\section[enfadado]{enfadado — angry, annoyed}

\label{lesson:ES-C707-enfadado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for panic, then the Spanish for to fear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: enfadado}
\textbf{enfadado} — \textquotedblleft{}angry, annoyed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi jefe está enfadado conmigo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My boss is angry with me.}
\end{quote}

The usual word in Spain: \emph{estar enfadado con alguien}. Latin America mostly uses another word, coming up next.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{enfadado} is built on \emph{enfadar}, which is usually traced to Portuguese \emph{enfadar}, made from \emph{fado} \textquotedblleft{}fate\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{fātum}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enfadado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enfadado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{enfadado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for panic, then the Spanish for to fear, then say \emph{enfadado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does enfadado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Angry, annoyed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enojado]{enojado — cross, angry}

\label{lesson:ES-C707-enojado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to fear, then the Spanish for angry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: enojado}
\textbf{enojado} — \textquotedblleft{}cross, angry\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¿Por qué estás enojada?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Why are you cross?}
\end{quote}

The everyday word in Latin America; in Spain people mostly say \emph{enfadado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{enojado} is built on \emph{enojar}, which is usually traced to spoken Latin \emph{inodiāre}, from the phrase \emph{in odiō} \textquotedblleft{}in hatred\textquotedblright{}; \emph{odio} comes from the same Latin word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enojado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enojado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{enojado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to fear, then the Spanish for angry, then say \emph{enojado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does enojado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Cross, angry\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la rabia]{la rabia — rage, fury; rabies}

\label{lesson:ES-C707-rabia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for angry, then the Spanish for cross.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la rabia}
\textbf{la rabia} — \textquotedblleft{}rage, fury; rabies\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me da rabia perder el autobús.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It makes me furious to miss the bus.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Me da rabia} — it makes me mad. The same word names the disease rabies.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rabia} is inherited from Latin \emph{rabiēs} \textquotedblleft{}rage, madness\textquotedblright{} through a spoken form \emph{rabia} (EtymDB); English \emph{rabies} and \emph{rabid} share it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la rabia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la rabia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la rabia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for angry, then the Spanish for cross, then say \emph{la rabia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la rabia mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Rage, fury; rabies\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[la ira]{la ira — anger, wrath}

\label{lesson:ES-C707-ira}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for cross, then the Spanish for rage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ira}
\textbf{la ira} — \textquotedblleft{}anger, wrath\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Habló con ira.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He spoke with anger.}
\end{quote}

A strong, written word; in conversation people say \emph{rabia} or \emph{enfado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ira} comes from Latin \emph{īra} \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), the source of English \emph{ire} and \emph{irate} too.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[fastidiar]{fastidiar — to annoy, to bother}

\label{lesson:ES-C707-fastidiar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for rage, then the Spanish for anger.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fastidiar}
\textbf{fastidiar} — \textquotedblleft{}to annoy, to bother\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me fastidia el ruido de la calle.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The street noise annoys me.}
\end{quote}

Works like \emph{gustar}: \emph{me fastidia}. \emph{¡No fastidies!} — You are kidding!

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fastidiar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{fastīdiāre} (\emph{fastīdiō}) \textquotedblleft{}to feel disgust, to loathe\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{fastīdium} \textquotedblleft{}loathing\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{fastidious} comes from the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fastidiar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fastidiar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fastidiar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for rage, then the Spanish for anger, then say \emph{fastidiar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
